source.value:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/343f6f32ac21a1bf06b86174734dd9ebba6ddb7598cbe83b4ade59f70e8e8b26.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/cb0f32e55af289452f1429ddfe3214a46501c55f3a61deaf10b4f736e47dca7f.png)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/85fdb4fc83a6f2b44178be2e97a0e7985d97350deb4e0fb123e513a80090906a.png)

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/3f984a493e976bd522455395defcb4c1562d61ca56e19fa27e2272832ce6011c.png)
must approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_1 < 0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/44f82894493c95c38039bc1e6a842bb7226571e9818e3c10c50d33627464ea37.png)
must also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_2 < 0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies $\lambda_1 < 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/f292220b15ff9b0d695cb8b9f2349cc275557fd2b77c32c147e25365ab0f7e47.png)

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/5671487738e750f488ad61852f17fb4b6b14cf4050fee66338000d4939914ce6.png)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/651cc55c8b96c402fc00140c06736493e71276666ce4eb1ba74c2294600a1b89.png)

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/222dcd944fc89cd0f07970cddf5c50aa167c7f2d25b1f7305779c3dbb0a4a6af.png)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/08ad54b92f62513fb88f12f7bd6da358263e46673d686e0982a1e8044b8ab131.png)
lie on the $y$-axis. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/c5b1aa6ccde39c56b503e2d59a56e2ac8058b08495567f4e2cb40f6a056faedd.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-{c}_{1}{e}^{-t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/6c3af2fe68c4bcddbbfd9f13eb84e73014511374c0adc570084f9c92773d31e0.png)

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/7f53fdda091242e4fee1edd70a7e96c649eff8bac93fcdc9fed6da38ec5c7523.png)

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/1ea46da3e9697ee89d1112dfec53457657271c391a28a6c55267da70d38157c4.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form

lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=4$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/85e8d745e2b504770815bb92ad1a151f422c941874f33840593836e78eeaacde.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2f67b02cda725daa0d0b994f3f4952065793e53ddc32260b14310f5158876f4f.png)
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{an unstable node (source)}}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2b79201d15fe5d2a9896cdee09c0474b97bb933d75fcf478c6fdb37cb4d16742.png)
